theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Existence and Attributes of God
doctrine: The Existence and Attributes of God
summary: God’s self-revelation in his names; communicable and incommunicable attributes; the holiness of God
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 3:13-15 and Exodus 34:5-7. The first passage is the revelation of God’s name at the burning bush. The second is God’s own description of his character, given after Israel’s sin with the golden calf. Read them together, and ask what each says about who God is.
settingTheScene: This is the first doctrinal pause in Unit 5. Each time you meet one of these days, you step back from the story and ask what the Bible teaches. Today the topic is the most basic one: who God is. You have just read the call of Moses, where God revealed his name and described himself as the God of the fathers. Now you look at the two most important self-descriptions in the Old Testament. One tells you that God exists on his own. The other tells you what God is like.
observation: Moses asks, “If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, The God of your fathers has sent me to you, and they ask me, What is his name? what shall I say to them?” (3:13).
God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” and “I AM has sent me to you” (3:14).
He then says, “The LORD, the God of your fathers…has sent me to you. This is my name forever” (3:15).
In Exodus 34, Moses is on Mount Sinai after Israel’s sin with the golden calf. The LORD passes before him and proclaims, “The LORD, the LORD” (34:6).
God describes himself as “a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (34:6).
He “keeps steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” (34:7).
But he is also one “who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children’s children, to the third and the fourth generation” (34:7).
Moses quickly bows his head and worships (34:8).
doctrinalFocus:
What is God like? The Bible’s answer starts with what theologians call his “aseity,” from a Latin phrase meaning “from himself.” God has life in himself. He does not need anything or anyone. He was not created, and nothing sustains him. When God says, “I AM WHO I AM,” he is saying, among other things, that he is the one who simply is. Everything else depends on him, and he depends on nothing. This is the foundation for all that follows. It means that God is not one more thing in the universe, even the greatest of them. He is the Creator of everything that is not himself.

The name given at the burning bush, written in English Bibles as “the LORD” in capital letters, is God’s personal name, Yahweh. It is related to the verb “to be,” and it speaks of his eternal, unchangeable presence. He is faithful to his promises because he does not change. Malachi 3:6 says, “For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed.” James 1:17 speaks of the “Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.” This is what theologians call God’s immutability. It does not mean that God is cold or distant. It means that his character and purposes are utterly reliable.

Then there is the self-description in Exodus 34:6-7, which becomes the most quoted passage in the Old Testament. Over and over, in the Psalms, the Prophets, and Nehemiah, writers return to these words (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). It is God’s own summary of his character. Notice how it starts: with mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love, and faithfulness. These are the words that come first. God’s character is, above all, a character of love. And yet the passage does not stop there. God “will by no means clear the guilty.” He is holy and just. His love is not weak, and his justice is not harsh.

Theologians sometimes divide God’s attributes into two groups. Some are incommunicable, meaning that they belong to God alone: his self-existence, his infinity, his unchangeableness, his omnipresence, his omniscience, his omnipotence. Others are communicable, meaning that human beings, made in his image, can reflect them in a limited way: love, mercy, justice, holiness, wisdom, faithfulness. This division helps explain why the Bible calls us to be like God (Ephesians 5:1) and also reminds us that he is infinitely beyond us.

The two attributes in tension in Exodus 34 are love and justice, and the rest of the Bible is the story of how they meet. How can a God who forgives iniquity also refuse to clear the guilty? The answer is not given here. It is given at the cross, where, as Paul writes, God is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The two halves of Exodus 34:7 are held together in Christ.
interpretation:
Look at the setting of each passage. The first comes at the beginning of God’s work of redemption, when he sends Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt. The second comes after Israel has broken the covenant by worshiping the golden calf. In the first, God’s name is an assurance that he will keep his promises. In the second, God’s character is his answer to the question that Israel’s sin raises: is it over?

God’s response to a failed covenant is to describe himself. He does not explain a method or lay out terms. He says who he is. “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious.” The ground for hope after sin is not that people will do better but that God is who he is. This is what makes grace possible.

It matters, too, that Moses bows and worships. A right knowledge of God does not lead to pride but to worship. If you ever study the doctrine of God and find it making you proud or merely curious, something has gone wrong. The right response is Moses’ response: to bow your head, and worship.

Finally, take note of the two kinds of statements in 34:7. They are not in contradiction. God is serious about sin because he is good. And he is willing to forgive because he is good. If he ignored sin, he would not be good. If he never forgave, he would not be merciful. The God of the Bible is both.
connection: Jesus claims the divine name in John 8:58 and says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). John 1:14 says that the Word “dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory…full of grace and truth,” echoing “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.” Paul writes that God put forward Christ “to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25).
application:
Try to describe God, in your own words, using the list in Exodus 34:6-7. Which attribute do you find easiest to believe? Which is harder?

If you find it hard to believe in God’s mercy, read these verses again, and notice that he said them about himself after Israel’s worst sin.

Pray the passage as a prayer: “LORD, you are merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.” Let it become your first thought about God.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for who he is: self-existing, unchanging, merciful, and just.
Thank him that in Jesus the name I AM is made known.
Tell him which of his attributes you most need to remember today.
